title: Voyager 1 Nears a One-Light-Day Milestone
summary:
Nearly 50 years after leaving Earth, NASA's Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone that shows just how far humanity's most distant spacecraft has traveled: a distance of one light-day from Earth, meaning light itself takes a full day to make the trip.

Keeping the aging explorer running has become harder as its power supply slowly fades. Both Voyager spacecraft make electricity from the heat released as plutonium decays, and each loses about 4 watts of generating capacity per year. After almost five decades, engineers have very little power to spare and have steadily shut down equipment that is no longer essential.

In September, the Voyager team completed a tricky energy-saving project nicknamed the "Big Bang," replacing three devices aboard Voyager 1 with alternatives that use less electricity. The devices help keep temperatures inside the spacecraft steady, and all three had to be replaced at once to keep heat distributed properly.

The upgrade should extend the working lives of Voyager 1's remaining scientific instruments. Without it, NASA might have had to shut down another instrument as early as summer 2027.

That matters because no other mission can take measurements from where Voyager 1 now travels. Launched in 1977, it has crossed beyond the Sun's heliosphere into interstellar space.

Even with the power upgrade, Voyager 1 keeps surprising its team. On October 18 and 19, NASA's Deep Space Network failed to receive its signal during two scheduled attempts. The signal unexpectedly returned on October 20, about 48 hours after the interruption began, and communication has held since.

Engineers found that one set of thrusters had stopped working and the spacecraft had automatically switched to backups, part of a built-in safety system. "We have to expect the unexpected," said mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.
why_it_matters: Voyager 1 is the only spacecraft measuring interstellar space, so every extra month it survives brings back knowledge nothing else can gather.

background_read: Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe launched in 1977 to study the outer planets, and it has kept flying ever since, becoming the most distant human-made object.
Spacecraft far from the Sun cannot rely on solar panels, so Voyager makes electricity from the heat of decaying plutonium — a supply that slowly weakens year by year.
Beyond the Sun's heliosphere lies interstellar space, the region between the stars, where Voyager's instruments take measurements no other spacecraft can.
